edge-ai: A cutaway view of a missile in its final seconds of flight reveals a tiny, low-power AI chip and compact camera housed inside its nose cone, where raw video is being processed locally into bright target-recognition outlines around a vehicle on the ground below while the missile’s fins autonomously adjust course; in the background, a distant data center fades on the horizon, connected to the weapon only by a broken, jammed radio link, visually insisting that the lethal computation happens entirely on board without any live cloud connection, and the stark miniature scale of the embedded hardware—contrasted with the massive, remote server racks—underscores the severe efficiency and size constraints that define the field.
system-on-module: A detailed cutaway centers on a credit-card-sized green circuit board—the system-on-module—its surface densely packed with a visible processor, memory modules, graphics chip, and storage, shown halfway inserted into a socket on a larger surrounding circuit board that bears partially completed traces for custom sensors, motors, and antennas. Behind this assembly, the composition splits into two mirrored worlds: on the left, stacks of identical modules sit in benign industrial lighting beside a warehouse robot, emphasizing mass production and low cost, while on the right, the exact same module is being installed into the cramped electronics bay of a silhouetted cruise missile or drone, so that a single visual glance conveys how the standardized, ready-to-use computing core travels effortlessly from civilian automation to military hardware.
